title: TMS for Depression: Does Brain Stimulation Really Work?
description: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation explained. How it works, success rates, cost, what to expect, and who's a good candidate for TMS treatment.

content.text: TMS uses magnetic pulses to stimulate brain regions involved in depression. It sounds like science fiction, but it's FDA-approved and covered by most insurance. Here's what you need to know.

A magnetic coil placed against your scalp delivers focused pulses to the prefrontal cortex—a region underactive in depression. These pulses stimulate neurons and, over multiple sessions, help normalize brain activity.

items: Targets the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Effects build gradually with repeated sessions

content.text: Meta-analyses show TMS achieves 50-60% response rate and 30-35% remission rate in treatment-resistant depression.
content.citation: Mutz et al., The Lancet Psychiatry, 2019

content.text: For context, these are patients who've failed multiple medications—a population where any treatment struggles.

items: Can read, watch videos during treatment
Most insurance covers after medication failures

content.text: TMS is a legitimate option for treatment-resistant depression with a solid evidence base. It's well-tolerated, non-invasive, and covered by most insurance after medication failures. The main barrier is the time commitment—36 sessions is a lot. But for people who haven't responded to medications, it's worth considering.
